# Discussion

We found the expected net global change effects, that diversity decreases with warming and nitrogen and increases with grazing, which is in line with many other studies [@klein2004experimental; @kaarlejarvi2017herbivores; @wu2020additive; @shangguan2024plant; @anderson2025experimental; @Austrheim2001-nu; @klein2004experimental; @niedrist2009plant; @Bernes2015-yg; @post2023large]. However, the magnitude and direction of the effect of the drivers was context dependent, with considerable differences between the alpine and sub-alpine communities. In this study, we take a step further by disentangling the direct and indirect effects of three global change drivers, to understand their underlying mechanisms and to generalize across drivers and climate context. Specifically, we tested whether these global change drivers all operate on diversity indirectly, mediated through community biomass, which reflects the magnitude and type of competition. If that were true, knowing general patterns and trends in community biomass of plants could predict changes in plant diversity rather than needing to understand all the direct effects of different drivers. 

We only found partial support for our hypothesis, with indirect effect through community biomass having substantial effects in the alpine community, but relatively little impact in the sub-alpine. In the sub-alpine community, warming and nitrogen addition affected diversity directly and also in the alpine, we found strong direct effects of warming. Below, we explore community biomass-mediated effects on diversity in this experiment, the mechanisms underlying the direct effects of each of the global change drivers, why these mechanisms might differ between alpine and sub-alpine communities. Finally, we discuss the implications for our ability to generalize impacts of global change drivers.

### Community biomass-mediates effects of global change on diversity

The SEMs show a negative indirect effect of all three global change drivers mediated through biomass in both communities, although it was only significant in the alpine (@fig-cut-final-diversity). Nevertheless, the environmental affinities suggest that community biomass plays an important role even at the sub-alpine community. The net indirect effect of the global change drivers on diversity and evenness tended to be negative, except for richness in the sub-alpine (Supplement Figure S6), suggesting a combination of shift in abundance of species with different competitive abilities and the gain or loss of species. For both communities, we see a significant shift towards less light demanding species with increasing community biomass, suggesting greater competition for light [e.g. @olsen2016facilitation]. A similar shift is evident in both communities for the warming and nitrogen addition treatments, which has been observed previously [@Klanderud2005-yx; @Wang2012-cj; @Fu2016-dw]. One possible explanation of the lack of significant biomass mediated effect on diversity at the sub-alpine community is that the alpine community was more temperature and nutrient limited and had more species to begin with compared to the sub-alpine community. The global change drivers had less impact on community biomass in the sub-alpine community (i.e. lower explanatory power in the regression model; @fig-1-biomass-diversity a), yielding a smaller range of biomass to manipulate. An alternative explanation is the likely non-linearity of the relationship between total plant biomass and the intensity of competition for light. In both communities, the biggest shift in the light affinity is at the highest levels of biomass or nitrogen, suggesting that changes in competitive interactions vary across environmental gradients (REFs). <!-- I don't understand this -->

Clipping and grazing effects on the diversity indices were always mediated through community biomass, except for a direct clipping effect on evenness at the sub-alpine. In line with many other studies, we found that clipping was able to prevent the loss of diversity and evenness under warming and nitrogen levels above 10 kg N ha^-1^ y^-1^ at the alpine community (@fig-1-biomass-diversity b), suggesting this was related to competitive release [@Austrheim2001-nu; @klein2004experimental; @niedrist2009plant; @Bernes2015-yg; @kaarlejarvi2017herbivores; @post2023large]. Interestingly, higher biomass and warming led to a shift to species with higher grazing tolerance in the alpine, but not in the sub-alpine community. In the same experiment, we have shown that warming shifts the alpine community to more resource acquisitive traits [@halbritter2025effects], suggesting a shift towards a community with a higher tolerance for grazing [@lebbink2024plant; @archibald2019unified].

### Direct effects of global change on diversity

Warming had a direct positive effect on diversity, species richness, and evenness in the alpine community (@fig-cut-final-diversity), which likely reflects a combination of shift in abundance towards more warm adapted species and colonization by species with a higher temperature requirements from the vegetation surrounding the transplanted community. This is supported by a strong shift in the temperature affinity with warming (@fig-toenails b). Contrary, at the sub-alpine community, warming had a strong negative direct effect on diversity and species richness, but without any accompanying shift in distribution of the temperature affinity. Interestingly, warming in the sub-alpine community also induced a shift towards more moisture demanding species, which was not observed in the alpine community. Overall, soil moisture was lower in the warmed communities of both sites (Supplement Figures 1 and 2, Supplement Table 1), however, in the last year of the experiment, warming had no effect on soil moisture at the boreal site (location of warmed sub-alpine communities). Soil moisture was however higher at the boreal site for parts of the growing season (Supplement Figure S1a), possibly because the taller and denser vegetation increase soil moisture (REF). The observed opposite patterns between the two communities might further be explained by an artifact of these communities. Warming shifted the alpine community towards warm demanding species which had a similar tolerance in moisture (@fig-toenails b). However, the sub-alpine plant community consisted of already highly temperature demanding species (i.e. high temperature affinities with narrow distribution), and warming therefore shifted the community towards species with a higher moisture tolerance (i.e. *Carex bigelowii,* *C. pilulifera*, and *Phleum alpinum* that have medium moisture affinities were lost). Overall, warming can have strong direct effects on plant diversity [@white2014direct].\
<!--Soilmoisture higher in denser veg. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S03418162130 -->

Nitrogen addition had a direct negative effect on diversity in both communities, but the effect was much stronger and significant at the sub-alpine. Nitrogen addition directly decreased evenness at the sub-alpine community, suggesting a shift in abundance of species with specific competitive abilities rather than loss of species. This is unlikely due to a shift in nutrient demanding species since such a shift only occurred in the alpine and was very small in the sub-alpine community. The environmental affinities however suggest that the strong direct effect of nitrogen addition is a consequence of acidification of fertilizing [@Kimmel2020-fo]. At both communities, there was a strong and significant shift towards more acid tolerant species with increasing nitrogen. The fertilization effect could have been stronger at the sub-alpine community, because it was less nutrient limited. In our study, this explanation is also supported by an increase in available calcium at high levels of nitrogen addition, which can be released from the bedrock under acid conditions. <!-- we have data from PRS probes to show that -->

Clipping and grazing had no direct effects on diversity, except that clipping decreased evenness directly at the sub-alpine site. Clipping and grazing must have affected diversity mostly through community biomass, as none of the environmental affinities showed any shifts due to clipping. The direct effect on evenness in the sub-alpine, was however not reflected in the environmental affinities that we measured. <!-- in which way? -->

### Interesting stuff about biomass and stronger T and N limitation in the alpine

Our main hypothesis was that the three global change drivers, warming, nitrogen addition, and clipping, operate through increased community biomass favoring more intense competition, especially for light, resulting in a decrease in vascular plant diversity. In line with the first part of this hypothesis, we found a strong increase in community biomass with warming and nitrogen addition in both alpine and sub-alpine communities, paralleling the findings of previous studies manipulating one or both of these drivers [@elmendorf2012plot; @Humbert2016-wg; @Zhang2023-xg]. Warming can increase biomass because of higher rates of photosynthesis, a longer growing season, or because higher microbial activity can increase nutrient availability, while nitrogen addition directly increases nutrient availability. The alpine site was strongly temperature and nutrient limited, resulting in a four to five times increase of community biomass with either warming or nitrogen addition. This co-limitation at the alpine site could be an explanation for the stronger mediation through biomass compared to the sub-alpine site. <!-- Last sentence, needs more explanation -->

-   Note that the warmed alpine and the unwarmed subalpine have very similar N slopes. They are living in the same climate! So even if the community is different, the N limitation is real at this temperature, but not when it is colder (or warmer).

### Conclusions and implications

Our findings show that community biomass can be used as a general indicator of mechanisms mediating global change impacts on plant diversity, but only in colder and unproductive alpine grasslands. Several of these drivers including warming, nitrogen addition, clipping, and grazing work through the same mechanisms. However, at the same time, we also found that some drivers including warming and nitrogen addition operate through multiple mechanisms. This means that only including community biomass only works partially, and might miss some of the direct effects.

The relative importance of the drivers was not consistent across sites, advocates for replicating experiments across gradients and landscapes to allow more general understanding of ecological processes [@fraser2013coordinated; @prager2022integrating]. Our results showed that community proxies, such as environmental affinities can help to get a more general understanding of the underlying ecological processes.

\[*is this useful?*\] Our study was conducted over three years and thus looks at short-term responses, which can differ from long-term responses[(*56*, *57*)](https://paperpile.com/c/KKq9O1/egX7+3xXg). Long-term experiments across different climatic contexts are needed to understand where and how local adaptation of grazing regimes can be used as a tool to mitigate impacts of warming and pollution and inform adaptive management strategies that benefit biodiversity.

The major change in community biomass, diversity and evenness occurred at levels of nitrogen addition beyond 10 kg N ha\^-1\^ y^-1^, which is the critical load for significant changes in the structure and function of alpine and sub-alpine grasslands (35). This similar relationship between the warmed alpine and ambient sub-alpine communities suggests that colder alpine plant communities are not intrinsically less productive than those at lower elevation, but are limited by temperature-related environmental factors (27).

Since the overall grazing effects were similar compared to clipping, it suggests that our simulated grazing treatment is comparable to natural grazing and that additional effects of grazing, such as different timing of biomass removal, trampling, and fertilization from the animals did not override the effect of biomass removal per se.

<!-- Interesting, but I don't see that this fits here -->

Interestingly, diversity indices based on change in abundance (i.e. evenness and diversity) showed more change in the cold alpine community in response to global change drivers, while indices based on change in species turnover (i.e. species richness and diversity), changed more in the warmer sub-alpine community. This might be because community changes in cold environments (i.e. the alpine) are often slow[(*45*)](https://paperpile.com/c/KKq9O1/ot2B) and changes in biomass (i.e. abundance) generally happen faster than species turnover (i.e. colonization or extinction) and there is often an extinction lag in alpine communities[(*14*, *15*, *46*)](https://paperpile.com/c/KKq9O1/ztDH+wbqE+5luD).
